turn_text: We have a guest with us on the Linder Farm Network, Brad Fenstad, who is running for Minnesota Congress and Minnesota's First District. And Brad, good to have you with us today. How's the campaigning going so far?

It's going great. It's like a big old family reunion everywhere I go traveling in Southern Minnesota. And just really blessed to call this area home and our families. My wife and I family have called Southern Minnesota home for generations. Great place to live and to work and to play and be honored to serve in Congress from this part of the state. So why
do you want to be a Congressman?

Yeah, so when I look at the world around us right now as a father of seven children and as a business owner and as a farmer, I've just grown up with that Southern Minnesota Norwegian teaching of whatever you're doing, leave it better than you found it. And I just feel like I can't sit back and watch what's happening. I just don't feel like our country is in a better place than I was gifted by my parents and grandparents and great-grandparents. So I feel called to step up and serve. All right,
let's talk about the big issues in your mind. And then we'll get to the ag issues. But overall, what would you see as the big issues this campaign will be circling around?

Yeah, so as I'm traveling across southern Minnesota, you know, I'm hearing a lot of discomfort and anxiety around the inflation that we're struggling with right now in the country. You know, when people are telling me they're going to the grocery store and buying a dozen eggs for $5 or a honey crisp apple for $1.90, that is really family pocketbook issues that we just can't have happen here in this country. You look at the gas prices, what we're paying at a pump, at the pump, and how that's affecting small businesses and interrupting some supply chain decisions based on costs. So the ripple effect that has in our economy and our backyard here in Southern Minnesota is very apparent. So it's keeping a lot of people up at night. They're worried about it. They're frustrated with it. And we just look back just two and a half years. And a lot of these problems and challenges didn't exist. And so we know leadership matters and we know that we can do better and we must do better.

turn_text: Brad, do you think there's a disconnect in Washington between what farmers and agriculture does and the people that are there?

Yeah, I do. I mean, I think everyone loves to eat, right? But no one No one really pays much attention out there to how the food is put on their plate and appreciate where it comes from. And quite frankly, the challenge is it takes to provide that to our country and the world. So there is a misunderstanding for just current practices. I look at farmers in southern Minnesota and just from an environmental standpoint how how innovative and how just amazing we've been with adapting and improving our technology and our practices. It rarely gets noticed by folks in Washington. We also are faced with challenges that I think are unique to the industry, unique to the country in regards to the workforce issues, shortage of workforce, the supply chain issues and, and quite frankly, the lack of leadership on the world stage, which has put us in a very vulnerable position from an input side. So when we look at, for instance, Urea and other fertilizer inputs, when we're seeing 200 to 400% increases in those inputs, that affects our bottom line. And you have folks in DC saying, well, the markets look great. Farmers are making money right now. And the reality is, yeah, the markets might be up, but what it's going to take to produce those bushels have gone up to and so the profits, the margins get ate up pretty quickly in that disruption in the supply chain and other global issues.

turn_text: You mentioned the whole energy situation. What do you feel about the impact that ethanol, biodiesel can have on our energy future?

And to be homegrown, America first, America made is a great energy policy, I think, just from a security standpoint, but also from an economic standpoint. We have some of the best, most efficient, effective farmers in the world right here in Southern Minnesota. And, you know, so for us to be have a seat at the table to be helpful in the energy crisis that we're in right now in regards to the cost side, you know, ethanol. I was happy to hear President Biden has changed his tune on the E-15 year-round mandate.
